description_full: Navigator Holdings Ltd. owns and operates a fleet of liquefied gas carriers worldwide. It engages in the international and regional seaborne transportation of petrochemical gases, liquefied petroleum gases, and ammonia for energy companies, industrial users, and commodity traders. The company also provides ship shore infrastructure and consultancy services. It operates through a fleet of 57 semi- or fully-refrigerated liquefied gas carriers. Navigator Holdings Ltd. was formerly known as Isle of Man public limited company and changed its name to Navigator Holdings Ltd. in 2006. The company was incorporated in 1997 and is based in London, the United Kingdom.

culture_narrative: Employs approximately 1K people. Revenue per employee of $297K ranks in the bottom quartile among Energy peers, improving at 8%/yr — growing workforce leverage. Each employee generates $59K of free cash flow annually. Stock-based compensation of $928 per employee reflects an ownership culture.
financial_summary: Navigator Holdings Ltd. is a small-cap energy business with a $1.2B market cap on $587M of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at +7% over the past three years and +6% annually across the full decade, a respectable pace for a business of this size.
Returns on capital run at 7% against a 8% cost of capital, which means the business is destroying value with every dollar it reinvests.

The business throws off $117M in free cash flow — roughly 20 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 2.01× so those profits are backed by real cash.

On the balance sheet, the balance sheet carries net cash, which is the gold standard: the business never has to make desperate decisions in a bad year, and thin 3.0× interest coverage leaves no room for a bad year.

Shareholder yield is only 1.2%, a thin return of capital, and insiders hold 42% of the shares, so management thinks like owners because it is one — the strongest alignment there is, and within its sector the business captures 2.6× its fair share of profits, a structural advantage visible in the numbers.

The sector is fragmented and competitive (HHI 0.05 across 202 companies in the universe; the top four hold 40% of revenue), so pricing power is hard to come by.
mkt: The shares are in a strong uptrend, up 37% over the past year excluding the latest month, though it has pulled back 6% over the last three months.
The price sits mid-way through its 52-week range, 22% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 32% and a beta of 0.68, it is more defensive than the market.

val: The stock trades 48% below its DCF fair value of $38.22, a meaningful margin of safety.
The fair-value models disagree (dispersion 59%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $31.38 to $47.92 (P10-P90), so treat the estimate as noisy.
On multiples it looks cheap against Energy peers: P/E 6.8 vs 13.4 and P/FCF 10.3 vs 14.3 (sector median).
Against its own history it is cheap: the EBIT multiple sits 37% below its 10-year median.
Earnings yields are attractive: an FCF yield of 9.7% (above the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 9.3% (vs the 8% bar).
The 6 covering analysts target $25.75 on average, 30% above the price, well away from the model's fair value.
prof: ROIC of 7% falls short of the cost of capital of 8.2%, so growth at these returns destroys value; returns have swung a lot from year to year (CV 0.69).
It converts 20% of revenue into free cash flow.
Earnings quality looks solid: a Piotroski score of 7/9 and cash conversion of 2.01x.
ROE of 8% comes mostly from margins and asset turnover rather than leverage (1.9x equity multiplier).
Operating margin is running 11pp above its own historical average, a peak-margin risk if conditions normalise.
It spends 0.3% of revenue on stock compensation.
hlth: The company holds more cash than debt.
Warning signs: an Altman Z of 1.49 in the distress zone, which caps the rating at HOLD.
growth: Revenue has compounded at 7.4% over 3 years, 12.0% over 5 years and 6.4% over 10 years, so growth is decelerating.
At current returns, reinvesting 64% of profits supports about 4.4% a year of fundamental growth, enough to sustain growth.
Forward indicators: a backlog worth 1.4x annual revenue and deferred revenue down 4%.
Capex runs only 0.6x depreciation (14.5% of sales), so the asset base is being harvested rather than grown.
Its Rule of 40 score is 32, below the 40 that marks a healthy growth business.
It has beaten earnings estimates by 27.3% on average.
own: Insiders own 41.6%, meaningful skin in the game, and institutions hold 45%.
Shareholder yield is a modest 1.2% (1.6% in dividends).
The share count has grown 3.1% a year over five years, diluting existing holders.
people: With about 1,975 employees, each generates about $297K of revenue, 0.1x the Energy median, and productivity has risen 7.8% a year.
That works out to $59K of free cash flow per employee.
